content: Bipolar disorder is a prevalent and severe mental health condition, affecting approximately 60 million individuals globally. It is characterized by significant fluctuations in mood, cognition, and behavior, which can severely impair an individual's functioning and quality of life. People with bipolar disorder are disproportionately affected by obesity compared to the general population. Research indicates that around 68% of individuals with bipolar disorder who seek treatment are either overweight or obese. Obesity in individuals with bipolar disorder is associated with an increased risk of developing other serious physical health conditions, such as diabetes, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and coronary heart disease. Among these, cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of premature mortality in this population, often occurring a decade or more earlier than in the general population. The factors contributing to this elevated risk include those related to the illness itself (e.g., mood episodes such as mania or depression), the side effects of treatments (e.g., weight gain from medications), and lifestyle factors (e.g., physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, smoking, and substance abuse). Various strategies have been proposed to manage obesity in individuals with bipolar disorder. These include non-pharmacological interventions such as dietary modifications, exercise programs, behavioral therapies, and multi-component approaches. Pharmacological interventions involve the use of weight loss medications or switching to medications with fewer weight-related side effects. Surgical options, such as gastric bypass, gastric banding, biliopancreatic diversion, and vertical banded gastroplasty, are also considered in some cases. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of these interventions in managing obesity among individuals with bipolar disorder. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Common Mental Disorders Controlled Trials Register (CCMDCTR), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycInfo, up to May 2020. Additional searches were performed in the World Health Organization (WHO) trials portal and ClinicalTrials.gov. Reference lists of relevant studies and systematic reviews were also examined. The inclusion criteria for this review were strict. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs), including individual, cluster, or cross-over designs, were eligible. At least 80% of the study participants had to have a clinical diagnosis of bipolar disorder and comorbid obesity (defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m² or higher). No restrictions were placed on the type of bipolar disorder, stage of illness, age, or gender. The interventions considered included dietary, exercise, behavioral, and multi-component approaches, as well as pharmacological and surgical interventions. Comparators included inactive controls for each type of intervention. The primary outcomes of interest were changes in body mass, patient-reported adverse events, and quality of life. Four authors were involved in the study selection process. Two authors independently screened the titles and abstracts of identified studies, and another two authors independently reviewed the full-text articles. However, none of the studies that were assessed met the inclusion criteria for this review. If studies had been included, their methodological quality would have been evaluated using the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Data would have been analyzed using risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes, with overall effect sizes calculated alongside 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Ultimately, no studies met the inclusion criteria, and the review was unable to determine the effectiveness of interventions for managing obesity in individuals with bipolar disorder. This highlights a significant gap in the evidence base and underscores the urgent need for high-quality research in this area. The authors recommend conducting randomized controlled trials specifically targeting populations with bipolar disorder and comorbid obesity. Several ongoing studies were identified, which may contribute to future updates of this review.
